title: REST API Design for Frontend Developers

subtopics.title: Resource and route
subtopics.explanation: A REST API exposes resources such as products or orders through URLs. A route identifies the resource. Use names that describe things, then use HTTP methods to describe actions. A library shelf is easier to search when each book has a clear label. For example, GET can read `/products/42`, while POST can create an order. A resource route is like a labeled shelf that helps people find one item.

subtopics.title: HTTP method
subtopics.explanation: GET usually reads data, POST creates or starts work, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, and DELETE removes. The method gives the request a shared meaning. Servers still need to validate every request. These verbs work like clear action labels on a form. For example, a POST request can create an order, while PATCH can change only its delivery address. For example, a PATCH request can change one field while preserving other resource values.

subtopics.title: Status and errors
subtopics.explanation: The response status summarizes the outcome. A 2xx status usually means success; 4xx points to a request or permission problem; 5xx indicates server trouble. Return a useful error shape so the page can show a next step. For example, if a product is missing, return a not-found status and a stable error message. For example, return validation details that let a form identify the field to correct. A status code is like a receipt marking whether an order was accepted.

subtopics.title: Pagination
subtopics.explanation: Large collections should arrive in manageable pieces. Pagination can use page numbers or continuation cursors. Keep sort and filter choices in the URL so a result can be shared and revisited. It is like reading one shelf at a time instead of moving the whole library. For example, a cursor can continue after the last result when new records arrive during pagination. For example, use stable cursor pagination for a list that changes while being browsed.

subtopics.title: Frontend states
subtopics.explanation: A request takes time and can fail. Show loading, success, empty, and error states; prevent duplicate actions when needed. Cancel obsolete searches so an old response cannot replace newer results. The page should guide users at every stop. For example, keep the previous search results visible or announce loading while a replacement request is pending. For example, cancel an old search request when a newer query replaces it. Loading, success, and error states are like stops along a delivery journey.

foundations.overview: REST-style APIs use URLs for resources and HTTP methods for actions.
foundations.whyItMatters: A predictable request contract helps the client respond to success, validation failures, and network problems. It also gives frontend and backend teams shared expectations.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser sends fetch requests and receives responses asynchronously. The UI must remain responsive while those requests are pending.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use typed request helpers, cancellation, explicit error handling, and URL-backed filters in production screens.
foundations.businessImpact: Stable API behavior lets teams change the interface without confusing users or losing work.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Document methods, status codes, pagination, and error shapes as a contract between frontend and server teams.
foundations.performanceImpact: Paginate large responses, cache safe reads, and cancel outdated requests.
commonUseCases: A product page loads one item with GET and sends an order with POST.
A search screen requests results in pages and preserves filters in the URL.
A form shows a useful message when the server rejects invalid input.
Fetch a product and display a not-found state when its ID is invalid.
Submit an order and show a retry path if the server reports a temporary failure.

commonMisconceptions.myth: REST means every API must use exactly one URL per database table.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Routes should represent useful resources for the client; server design and domain boundaries may require several related routes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A 200 response means the requested action succeeded.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The client must interpret the status and response body; application errors can still be represented in a successful transport response.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser can enforce access by hiding a button.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The server must authenticate and authorize every protected request because users can call an endpoint without the page UI.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every REST response must use one exact JSON shape.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Choose a consistent contract for each resource and document error responses so clients can recover.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Pagination is only needed after the page becomes slow.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Large payloads waste bandwidth and memory; define result limits before collections grow.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The frontend can decide whether a request is authorized.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The server must check identity and permission for every protected action.
